theory.overview: Autoencoders are neural networks that learn to copy their input to their output through a compressed representation. By forcing data through an information bottleneck, they learn efficient encodings of input data—useful for dimensionality reduction, denoising, anomaly detection, and generative modeling. Unlike other dimensionality reduction techniques like PCA, autoencoders can learn non-linear transformations, capturing complex patterns in data.

sections.title: The Encoder-Decoder Architecture
sections.content: Autoencoders consist of two parts: an encoder compresses input into a latent representation (bottleneck), and a decoder reconstructs the input from this representation.

sections.title: Undercomplete Autoencoders
sections.content: The simplest form with a bottleneck smaller than the input. Forces the network to learn the most salient features.
properties: Risk: learning identity function if bottleneck too large

sections.title: Denoising Autoencoders
sections.content: Trained to reconstruct clean input from corrupted version. Learn robust features that capture essential structure.
sections.training: Input: corrupted x' (e.g., with Gaussian noise or dropout). Target: clean x.
sections.benefit: Cannot simply memorize—must learn underlying patterns

sections.title: Sparse Autoencoders
sections.content: Instead of compressing dimension, enforce sparsity constraint on hidden activations. Many neurons inactive for any given input.
sections.intuition: Like having many specialists—each neuron learns to detect specific features

sections.title: Variational Autoencoders (VAE)
sections.content: Probabilistic autoencoders that learn a distribution over latent space. Enable sampling new data points.
components: Encoder outputs μ and σ (parameters of latent distribution)
Reparameterization trick: z = μ + σ·ε where ε ~ N(0,1)
sections.advantage: Smooth, structured latent space—interpolation produces meaningful variations

sections.title: Applications
sections.content: Autoencoders have diverse practical applications across domains.

uses.comparison: Non-linear PCA, better for complex manifolds

uses.approach: Denoising autoencoder learns to remove corruption

uses.benefit: Learned compression better than generic algorithms

keyConcepts.name: Bottleneck
keyConcepts.description: The compressed latent representation. Size determines information capacity.
keyConcepts.tradeoff: Smaller = more compression, harder to reconstruct accurately

keyConcepts.name: Reconstruction Loss
keyConcepts.description: Measures difference between input and output.

keyConcepts.name: Latent Space
keyConcepts.description: The compressed representation space. In VAEs, this follows a learned distribution.
keyConcepts.property: Nearby points in latent space should produce similar outputs

keyConcepts.name: KL Divergence
keyConcepts.description: In VAEs, measures how much the learned distribution differs from prior (usually N(0,I)).

complexity.training: $O(N \cdot E \cdot d^2)$ where N = samples, E = epochs, d = max layer size
complexity.inference: $O(d^2)$—single forward pass through encoder or decoder

steps.title: Input Corruption (Denoising)
steps.description: Add noise to input for denoising training.

steps.title: VAE: Sample Latent
steps.description: For VAE, sample from learned distribution.

practiceProblems.title: Bottleneck Size
practiceProblems.description: If input is 28×28 MNIST images (784 dims) and bottleneck is 32 dims, what's the compression ratio?
practiceProblems.explanation: The autoencoder compresses 784 pixel values into just 32 latent values—a 24.5x reduction. The decoder must learn to reconstruct from this highly compressed representation.

practiceProblems.title: Denoising vs Standard
practiceProblems.description: Why can't a denoising autoencoder simply learn to ignore its input and output the average of all training data?
practiceProblems.answer: Because different corrupted inputs map to different clean targets. The network must use structure in the corrupted input to determine what noise to remove.
practiceProblems.explanation: If the noise is random each time, the same underlying image produces different corrupted versions. To minimize loss across all these variations, the network must extract robust features that identify the underlying image, then reconstruct it.

practiceProblems.title: VAE Reparameterization
practiceProblems.description: Why use z = μ + σε instead of sampling z ~ N(μ, σ²) directly?
practiceProblems.answer: Backpropagation cannot flow through random sampling. The reparameterization trick moves sampling to an input noise variable, allowing gradients to flow through μ and σ.
practiceProblems.explanation: If we sample z directly from a distribution with learned parameters, we break the computation graph. By expressing z as a deterministic function of μ, σ, and fixed random noise ε, we enable gradient descent on μ and σ.
hints: Need gradients for μ and σ

practiceProblems.title: KL Loss Behavior
practiceProblems.description: If encoder outputs μ=0, σ=1 for all inputs, what is KL divergence from N(0,I)?
practiceProblems.explanation: When μ=0 and σ=1, the posterior q(z|x) equals the prior p(z)=N(0,I). The KL formula evaluates to zero, meaning no penalty. This is actually problematic—all inputs map to same distribution, losing distinctiveness.

practiceProblems.title: Anomaly Detection
practiceProblems.description: Design an anomaly detection system using autoencoders. What threshold should you use?
practiceProblems.answer: Train on normal data only. Set threshold as percentile (e.g., 95th) of reconstruction errors on validation set. New data with error > threshold = anomaly.
practiceProblems.explanation: Autoencoders learn to reconstruct 'normal' patterns well. Anomalous patterns—never seen in training—have high reconstruction error because the encoder compresses them into the 'normal' latent space poorly.

practiceProblems.title: Sparse vs Undercomplete
practiceProblems.description: Compare sparse autoencoders (many hidden units, sparsity constraint) vs undercomplete (few hidden units).
practiceProblems.answer: Undercomplete: hard bottleneck limit. Sparse: many units but few active simultaneously. Sparse can represent more diverse features—different subsets for different inputs.
practiceProblems.explanation: Undercomplete forces all information through fixed small vector. Sparse allows overcomplete representation (more units than inputs) but each input uses only a few. Like having many specialists vs few generalists.

codeExample.code:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

class Autoencoder(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_dim=784, hidden_dims=[256, 64], latent_dim=32):
        super().__init__()
        
        # Encoder
        encoder_layers = []
        prev_dim = input_dim
        for h_dim in hidden_dims:
            encoder_layers.extend([
                nn.Linear(prev_dim, h_dim),
                nn.ReLU(),
                nn.BatchNorm1d(h_dim)
            ])
            prev_dim = h_dim
        encoder_layers.append(nn.Linear(prev_dim, latent_dim))
        self.encoder = nn.Sequential(*encoder_layers)
        
        # Decoder (reverse architecture)
        decoder_layers = []
        prev_dim = latent_dim
        for h_dim in reversed(hidden_dims):
            decoder_layers.extend([
                nn.Linear(prev_dim, h_dim),
                nn.ReLU(),
                nn.BatchNorm1d(h_dim)
            ])
            prev_dim = h_dim
        decoder_layers.extend([
            nn.Linear(prev_dim, input_dim),
            nn.Sigmoid()  # For normalized [0,1] data
        ])
        self.decoder = nn.Sequential(*decoder_layers)
    
    def forward(self, x):
        z = self.encoder(x)
        x_recon = self.decoder(z)
        return x_recon, z

class DenoisingAutoencoder(Autoencoder):
    """
    Same architecture, different training procedure
    """
    def add_noise(self, x, noise_factor=0.3):
        noise = torch.randn_like(x) * noise_factor
        return torch.clamp(x + noise, 0, 1)

class VAE(nn.Module):
    """
    Variational Autoencoder with reparameterization trick
    """
    def __init__(self, input_dim=784, hidden_dim=400, latent_dim=20):
        super().__init__()
        
        # Encoder outputs mu and log_var
        self.fc1 = nn.Linear(input_dim, hidden_dim)
        self.fc_mu = nn.Linear(hidden_dim, latent_dim)
        self.fc_logvar = nn.Linear(hidden_dim, latent_dim)
        
        # Decoder
        self.fc_decode1 = nn.Linear(latent_dim, hidden_dim)
        self.fc_decode2 = nn.Linear(hidden_dim, input_dim)
    
    def encode(self, x):
        h = F.relu(self.fc1(x))
        return self.fc_mu(h), self.fc_logvar(h)
    
    def reparameterize(self, mu, logvar):
        """
        Reparameterization trick: z = mu + sigma * epsilon
        where epsilon ~ N(0, 1)
        """
        std = torch.exp(0.5 * logvar)
        eps = torch.randn_like(std)
        return mu + eps * std
    
    def decode(self, z):
        h = F.relu(self.fc_decode1(z))
        return torch.sigmoid(self.fc_decode2(h))
    
    def forward(self, x):
        mu, logvar = self.encode(x)
        z = self.reparameterize(mu, logvar)
        x_recon = self.decode(z)
        return x_recon, mu, logvar

def vae_loss(x_recon, x, mu, logvar):
    """
    VAE loss = Reconstruction loss + KL divergence
    """
    # Reconstruction loss (binary cross-entropy)
    BCE = F.binary_cross_entropy(x_recon, x, reduction='sum')
    
    # KL divergence: -0.5 * sum(1 + log(sigma^2) - mu^2 - sigma^2)
    KLD = -0.5 * torch.sum(1 + logvar - mu.pow(2) - logvar.exp())
    
    return BCE + KLD, BCE, KLD

# Training example
def train_autoencoder(model, dataloader, epochs=10, learning_rate=1e-3, device='cuda'):
    optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=learning_rate)
    model.to(device)
    
    for epoch in range(epochs):
        total_loss = 0
        for batch_idx, (data, _) in enumerate(dataloader):
            data = data.view(data.size(0), -1).to(device)
            
            # For denoising autoencoder, add noise here
            # noisy_data = model.add_noise(data) if isinstance(model, DenoisingAutoencoder) else data
            
            optimizer.zero_grad()
            
            if isinstance(model, VAE):
                recon_batch, mu, logvar = model(data)
                loss, bce, kld = vae_loss(recon_batch, data, mu, logvar)
            else:
                recon_batch, z = model(data)
                loss = F.mse_loss(recon_batch, data)
            
            loss.backward()
            optimizer.step()
            
            total_loss += loss.item()
        
        avg_loss = total_loss / len(dataloader.dataset)
        print(f'Epoch {epoch+1}/{epochs}, Loss: {avg_loss:.4f}')

# Feature extraction example
def extract_features(model, dataloader, device='cuda'):
    """
    Use trained encoder as feature extractor
    """
    model.eval()
    features = []
    labels = []
    
    with torch.no_grad():
        for data, target in dataloader:
            data = data.view(data.size(0), -1).to(device)
            if isinstance(model, VAE):
                mu, _ = model.encode(data)
                z = mu
            else:
                _, z = model(data)
            features.append(z.cpu())
            labels.append(target)
    
    return torch.cat(features), torch.cat(labels)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Test architectures
    print("=== Autoencoder Architectures ===\n")
    
    # Standard
    ae = Autoencoder(input_dim=784, hidden_dims=[256, 64], latent_dim=32)
    print(f"Standard AE: {sum(p.numel() for p in ae.parameters()):,} parameters")
    
    # VAE
    vae = VAE(input_dim=784, hidden_dim=400, latent_dim=20)
    print(f"VAE: {sum(p.numel() for p in vae.parameters()):,} parameters")
    
    # Test forward
    x = torch.randn(4, 784)
    
    ae_recon, z_ae = ae(x)
    print(f"\nStandard AE: input {x.shape} → latent {z_ae.shape} → output {ae_recon.shape}")
    
    vae_recon, mu, logvar = vae(x)
    print(f"VAE: input {x.shape} → latent (μ,σ) {mu.shape} → output {vae_recon.shape}")
    
    loss, bce, kld = vae_loss(vae_recon, x, mu, logvar)
    print(f"VAE loss: {loss.item():.2f} (BCE: {bce.item():.2f}, KL: {kld.item():.2f})")
